title: How much is left when five ninths go from seven ninths?
description: A strip is cut into nine equal parts and seven of them are shaded. Five shaded parts are taken away, and we check whether the answer can be made smaller.
teaching_notes: One idea: when two fractions count the same size of part, take away the top numbers, keep the bottom number, then check whether the answer is already in lowest terms. Watch for students who divide the top and the bottom when they share no factor.

video_script.why: The child takes away fractions that count the same fractional unit by taking away parts of one strip, then checks that the answer is already in lowest terms.
video_script.substitution: The same rectangular strip as the book's solved question about sevenths, now cut into nine equal parts.
video_script.anchor: a rectangular strip cut into nine equal parts with seven parts shaded, as in the book
video_script.payoff_line: Seven ninths take away five ninths leaves two ninths
video_script.fraction_reading: seven ninths, five ninths, one ninth, two ninths, five sevenths, two sevenths, three sevenths
never_show: the remaining fraction before the answer beat
maths_rules: the strip is cut into 9 equal parts, so each part is 1/9; 7/9 is 7 shaded parts
7/9 and 5/9 count the same fractional unit 1/9, so the numerators are taken away: 7 − 5 = 2
2 and 9 share no factor except 1, so 2/9 is in lowest terms
check: 2 parts left + 5 parts taken away = 7 parts, which is 7/9
ground demo: 5/7 − 2/7 = 3/7 on a strip of 7 equal parts
video_script.design: One idea: same size of part, take away the tops, keep the bottom, then check lowest terms. The strip stays on the board from start to end.
